title: Digital literacy and post truth challenges in the rural academic ecosystem of Tamil Nadu
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study of rural and semi-urban higher education in Tamil Nadu whose main survey (n = 284: 240 students, 44 faculty) asked how often respondents encounter false or misleading information on academic topics through digital platforms. It reports a share of respondents above a threshold - 60% (n = 170) encountered false or misleading academic content, i.e. at least 'occasionally' - which is a RECALL-exposure estimate with a stated denominator. The rest of the paper (device access, connectivity, trust, fact-checking habits, focus groups, institutional content analysis) is out of scope.

estimates.platform: Digital platforms generally; respondents named WhatsApp, YouTube and social media pages
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed students and faculty who reported encountering false or misleading academic content on digital platforms
estimates.denominator: 284 survey respondents (240 students, 44 faculty) recruited from twelve rural and semi-urban higher education institutions in Tamil Nadu; 78% response rate (284/364)
estimates.definition: Answered the frequency item 'How often do you encounter false or misleading information on academic topics through digital platforms?' at or above the 'occasionally' threshold; the Discussion phrases the same figure as having 'come across false or misleading academic materials through institutional channels' and the abstract as 'academic content that was inaccurate or unconfirmed'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition. The operative wording is the questionnaire item itself: "How often do you encounter false or misleading information on academic topics through digital platforms?"; the abstract broadens it to content "that was inaccurate or unconfirmed"
estimates.source_quote: 5.5.4 Survey findings (n = 284) Misinformation Exposure: 60% (n = 170) reported encountering false or misleading academic content.
estimates.page_loc: Section 5.5.4 'Survey findings (n = 284)', pp. 16-17; also Section 5.5.1 p. 16, the Discussion p. 20 and the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Wholly respondent-judged: no claim, source list or coder defines what counts as false or misleading; the respondent decides. No verification of the reported encounters and no reliability statistic for the survey instrument is reported (Section 3.4.1 on 'Survey instrument reliability' is truncated mid-sentence in the published text and gives no coefficient).
estimates.moderator_quote: Twelve remote and semi-urban higher education institutions in Tamil Nadu, including government, aided and autonomous colleges, were used to recruit participants. ... There were 284 responders in all, including 44 faculty members and 240 students. ... The primary poll had a 78% overall response rate (284/364)
estimates.notes: Confidence medium, not high. The 60% is stated consistently in four places (abstract, 5.5.1, 5.5.4, Discussion) and n = 170 reproduces it against 284, so the value itself is solid. But the paper's numbers are pervasively rounded to multiples of 5 or 10 and several are internally inconsistent (see missed_or_uncertain), the exact response option that defines the threshold is never printed, and the sample is voluntary and self-selected from twelve purposively chosen colleges - the authors themselves flag over-representation of the digitally confident. population_scope is 'other' because the frame is an academic population (undergraduates plus faculty), not a general-public sample; topic is 'other' because the referent is academic/educational subject matter rather than news, health or politics.

missed_or_uncertain: The platform breakdown was deliberately NOT extracted, and this is the main judgement call. Section 5.5.4 prints 'Platforms identified: WhatsApp (40%, n = 114), YouTube (30%, n = 85), social media pages (20%, n = 57)', with n values computed against the full 284. Those n values cannot be right: 40+30+20 = 90% of 284 would mean 256 respondents named a platform while only 170 reported any exposure at all. Read instead as shares of the 170 exposed, the arithmetic closes exactly (0.40+0.30+0.20 = 0.90 of 170 = 153, leaving 10% unspecified), which also matches the prose in 5.5.1: '60% have come across erroneous academic material, primarily on social media (20%), YouTube (30%) and WhatsApp (40%)'. So these are a within-exposed 'where did you see it' breakdown, not platform-specific prevalence shares, and extracting them at either denominator would import the author's arithmetic error. Also not extracted: (1) '45% (n = 36)' of the 81 certificate-course completers who 'admitted to previously sharing unverified academic content' - sharing without verifying is not sharing misinformation (a wholly true item earns the same label), so it fails the falsity condition; the same figure appears in 5.1 as '45% admitted sharing unverified academic material on WhatsApp/Google Classroom'. (2) '80% (n = 65)' reporting improved digital confidence after training - a training-effect outcome. (3) Fact-checking habits (20% always / 60% sometimes / 20% rarely verify) and 'Only 30% of respondents thoroughly check their sources' - verification behaviour, and the 20% and 30% versions contradict each other. (4) Trust figures (50% trust college LMS, 30% NPTEL, 60% distrust YouTube influencers) - trust, not exposure. (5) '50% of respondents acknowledge that emotional content influences their beliefs' and '40% acknowledge that digital content has a greater emotional impact' - belief/susceptibility, explicitly excluded. (6) '60% lacked training in identifying misinformation' (5.1) - a training gap. (7) Device, connectivity and opportunity/challenge percentages - infrastructure. (8) The Literature review's 'Digital Empowerment Foundation found that 60% of rural users struggled to distinguish credible from fake news' and Thangavel and Rajeshwari's '30% of students used technology daily' are figures cited from other studies, barred by R8. (9) The content analysis of LMS portals, WhatsApp academic groups and recommended YouTube lectures is reported purely qualitatively ('WhatsApp group forwards frequently included unverified notes and summaries') with no sample size and no share, so it yields no CONTENT row.

rob.design: Mixed-methods, single-author study. Main quantitative arm: structured questionnaire administered online (Google Forms) and on paper between June and September 2024 to students and faculty at twelve purposively selected rural/semi-urban colleges in Tamil Nadu; 284 of 364 returned usable responses (78%), 240 students (mean age 19.8, 52% female) and 44 faculty (mean 12 years' experience). Participation voluntary, hence self-selected. Qualitative arms: six focus groups (38 participants, 60-90 min, thematically coded) and an unquantified content analysis of college LMS portals, academic WhatsApp groups and faculty-recommended YouTube lectures. A separate certificate-course cohort (n = 81 of 88 enrolled, September 2024) provided pre/post surveys used only for triangulation and never merged with the main survey. No inter-coder reliability, no scale validation and no Cronbach's alpha are reported - the section headed 'Survey instrument reliability' breaks off mid-sentence. All prevalence figures are self-reported; the authors acknowledge recall error, social-desirability bias in exactly the misinformation items, and non-representativeness beyond rural Tamil Nadu.
